text.p: Aluminium prices slumped overnight on aggressive selling from one party and after a rise in stocks, before recovering somewhat to close US$15 down at US$1,455 a tonne.
Copper prices fell in sympathy, but nickel prices continued to rally. Gold prices slipped further, but support is seen from Australian buying.
Oil prices ended higher again on new Iraq concerns, while wheat prices also strengthened on higher exports. Sugar prices closed largely unchanged.
The CRB index closed up 0.50 of a point at 248.14.
METALS
Aluminium prices managed to recover some early losses by the afternoon kerb close on the London Metal Exchange (LME) Tuesday, but the probe lower has left the market looking vulnerable, traders said.
Copper also dipped towards key support before bouncing, while nickel extended its recent impressive rally.
Three month aluminium futures fell to a two-month low of $1,455 a tonne at one stage during the morning session, pushed lower by aggressive sales from one ring dealing quarter.
But the market recovered to finish the day at $1,462, still down $15 from Monday's afternoon kerb close.
Traders viewed the bounce as far from convincing, and some were braced for a break of the key support level soon.
"Everyone sold out and then a sniff of buying came in which prompted light covering. But the bounce is certainly not that convincing," said one LME floor trader.

Dealers said there was no fresh news to prompt Tuesday's wave of selling, although another rise in LME stocks of 4,700 tonnes did not help. Stocks have risen steadily to 947,625 tonnes from a low of 523,175 tonnes in October last year.

But data from the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) was slightly more positive, showing that world producer stocks in July fell 33,000 tonnes to 3.342 million tonnes from end-June levels.
Some analysts had been expecting a rise in IPAI stocks as producers used the slow summer demand period to re-stock.
Copper prices fell to $1,910 at one stage, a shade above the key support band pegged at $1,900/05.
But values rallied to finish at $1,924, down just $3 from Monday's close. Traders said the fall in stocks of 2,525 tonnes lent some support throughout the day.
Nickel ended stronger, gaining $85 to $7,700 to end towards the top end of the day's range between $7,570 to $7,730.
The market has risen over 11 percent from the low of $6,910 hit in early August.
Physical offtake is still generally slow, but traders said there was nervousness ahead of the labour contract expiry at Inco's Manitoba plant on September 15.
There were also rumours of delays to shipments from the giant Russian producer Norilsk adding to uncertainty.
But traders said the main spur to the market recently was speculative and fund buying of futures and call options.
Zinc fell when the markets were racing lower during the morning session, but failed to make up the losses. Prices finished $10.50 lower at $1,022.50.
GOLD
New York precious metals futures ended mixed on moderate volumes Tuesday, holding above Monday's intraday lows, with the exception of palladium which saw fresh life-of-contract lows.
"Gold and silver look oversold after 10 days of falls and we may see a bounce back above $385.00 basis spot, where it's likely we may see some producer selling to lock in the contango,
in case gold tests support around $380 again," Mitsui & Co USA bullion dealer, Greg Drury said.
"But there may be some producer buybacks from Australian miners down around $381 which could provide support."
COMEX December gold ended down 40 cents at $386.80 an ounce, after finding support at the session lows at $386.00.

In New York bullion trade, spot gold was quoted $383.00/383.40 at the close, compared to the London afternoon fix at $383.10. Earlier gold had fixed at a fresh two month low of $382.45 in London. New York bullion was quoted $383.40/383.80 at the close Monday.
OIL
NYMEX October crude ended Tuesday at a closing high after heightened tension in Iraq propelled the oil complex higher, traders said.
"There were reports that Iraqi troops were massing in the south and that just set off a round of buying," said Jim Ritterbusch, a trader with Sweeney Oil.
October crude settled up 39 cents at $24.12 a barrel, after almost reaching its life-of-contract high of $24.25.
"We should break it (the life-of-contract high) within a few
days," said Ritterbusch.
The next level of resistance is pegged at around $24.75.

Earlier Tuesday, a U.S. defense official denied a report citing Shiite muslim groups' claims that Iraq was massing troops near its southern border. Meanhwile, Iraq said it fired missiles at U.S. planes policing the southern no-fly zone.
While uncertainty surrounding the Iraqi conflict is supporting crude prices, traders said crude's price direction Wednesday will depend in part on this evening's API data.
WHEAT
CHICAGO - CBOT wheat futures closed higher on firm cash basis markets, an increase in exports and on follow-through technical buying from Monday's rally, traders said.
"They had gotten short and are covering, that's all it is," a trader said.
USDA's weekly export inspections report Monday was bullish to futures prices and traders also cited the lack of deliveries on the September as helping fuel gains.
A strong rally in soybean futures also boosted wheat, the traders said.
Wheat closed 3-3/4 to eight cents per bushel higher, with
September up eight at $4.61-1/2 a bushel.
SUGAR
CSCE world sugar futures ended unchanged to slightly higher Tuesday, lifted by trade buying, floor sources said.
October sugar finished up 0.02 cent a lb, at 12.05 cents, after ranging between 12.07 and 11.96. March ended unchanged, at 11.73, while the back months closed 0.02 to 0.09 higher.
